common_name: Illusion Garnet Lace Sweet Potato Vine (Finely Cut Burgundy Lacy-Leaf Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Garnet Lace is the deep burgundy-purple counterpart to Illusion Emerald Lace, sharing the same finely dissected, ferny leaf shape.

directions: Illusion Garnet Lace bears the same finely dissected, almost ferny leaf shape as its sibling Illusion Emerald Lace, but in a deep burgundy-purple that reads very differently in a container from the broad, solid leaves of cultivars like Blackie or Sweet Caroline Bronze. Its airy, lacy texture and dark color combine to give mixed containers and hanging baskets a softer, more intricate look than heavier-leaved ornamental sweet potato vine selections, while still trailing and filling in just as vigorously through summer heat. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — more sun deepens the burgundy coloring, while partial shade keeps the color slightly softer. It needs only occasional trimming to stay in scale with companion plants.

common_name: Purple Knight Alternanthera (Deep Purple-Black Heat-Loving Foliage Plant)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; Purple Knight grows taller and more upright than the compact Little Ruby, reaching 2-3 feet and useful as a dramatic dark-foliage accent in the middle of a bed or large container.

directions: Purple Knight is grown entirely as a foliage plant, valued for large, glossy leaves in an intense, near-black purple that deepens rather than fades in the hottest, most humid part of summer, unlike most dark-foliage plants that lose color intensity in extreme heat. Its taller, more upright habit than the compact Little Ruby cultivar makes it a striking vertical accent in mixed beds, large containers, and cutting gardens, where its stems are sometimes used in fresh arrangements for their dramatic color. Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinching young growth encourages fuller, more branched plants. The small white flowers are inconspicuous and add nothing ornamentally, so many gardeners shear the plant lightly through the season to keep energy directed into fresh, richly colored foliage.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Alternanthera for Florida Landscapes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Foliage Annuals for Gulf Coast
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heat-Tolerant Foliage Plants

common_name: Mojave Tangerine Portulaca (Large-Flowered Drought-Tolerant Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mojave was bred for notably larger, more weather-resistant flowers than older moss rose seed strains, on a mounding rather than trailing habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rich or consistently wet soil promotes rot and reduces flowering in this extremely drought-tolerant succulent annual. Mojave Tangerine produces unusually large, bright tangerine-orange flowers relative to older moss rose seed strains, held over fleshy, needle-like foliage on a compact, mounding plant well suited to the front of a border, rock garden, or hot, dry container planting. Like other portulaca, flowers open fully only in bright sun and close on cloudy days and in the evening, providing a long season of color from early summer through frost with minimal care. It thrives on neglect once established and needs very little supplemental water even through the hottest, driest stretch of a Gulf South summer.
